forces: Wind ensemble with contrabassoon and double bass
performers: United States Marine Band; Timothy Foley
recorded: 5–9 June 2000, Center for the Arts, George Mason University, Fairfax, Virginia
intro: The overture to Guillaume Tell has four sections: a slow dawn, an Alpine storm, a shepherd’s song and a gallop. The United States Marine Band plays a nineteenth-century wind transcription attributed to Wenzel Sedlak, in which bassoons and horns take over the parts of an opera orchestra.

cues.title: Opening, low wind
cues.text: The overture opens slowly, with interweaving low melodies. Rossini gave this music to five solo cellos. In this wind version the bass comes from bassoons, contrabassoon and double bass.
cues.evidence: Orrin Howard’s LA Phil note describes the five solo cellos. Frank P. Byrne’s Grand Scenes booklet identifies this transcription and the added contrabassoon and string bass; its personnel list identifies the two bassoonists. https://www.laphil.com/works/william-tell-overture; https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Audio/Educational_Series/grand_scenes/grand_scenes.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performance, Paris Opéra, 1829
cues.text: Guillaume Tell opened at the Paris Opéra on 3 August 1829. It is an opera in four acts about Swiss rebels resisting Austrian rule, and it includes Tell’s ordeal with the apple. The first act is set in a village in the canton of Uri.
cues.evidence: Rossini Opera Festival’s work history and synopsis give the première, four-act form and Swiss setting. https://www.rossinioperafestival.it/en/stories/guillaume-tell/

cues.title: The storm
cues.text: The storm begins. Quick, unsettled figures replace the long phrases of the opening, and the winds build gradually to a louder, fuller sound.
cues.evidence: Frank P. Byrne’s Grand Scenes booklet identifies the overture’s four scenes, including the Alpine storm, in the wind transcription performed here. https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Audio/Educational_Series/grand_scenes/grand_scenes.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ranz des vaches
cues.text: A broad tune returns the music to calm, and the flute plays decorations above it. This is the ranz des vaches, a Swiss herdsman’s call, with long notes below and quick ornaments over them.
cues.evidence: Byrne identifies the ranz des vaches and the adapted flute part; Orrin Howard describes the melody and flute decorations in Rossini’s original. The Commons source identifies this section from 5:14. https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Audio/Educational_Series/grand_scenes/grand_scenes.pdf; https://www.laphil.com/works/william-tell-overture
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fanfare and final march
cues.text: A fanfare introduces the final march. The galloping rhythm returns repeatedly beneath the tune until the overture’s close.
cues.evidence: Byrne describes the final fanfare and revolutionary march. Commons identifies the finale from 7:30 in this recording. https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Audio/Educational_Series/grand_scenes/grand_scenes.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Brno source and Marine Band edition
cues.text: The arrangement survives in a fifteen-movement Tell suite from the Augustinian monastery in Brno. For this recording the Marine Band adapted the flute part, removed two added trumpet parts and reinforced the bass with contrabassoon and double bass.
cues.evidence: Frank P. Byrne, Grand Scenes booklet, William Tell entry, PDF pages 5–6. The attribution to Wenzel Sedlak is qualified in the booklet. https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Audio/Educational_Series/grand_scenes/grand_scenes.pdf

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: United States Marine Band (wind ensemble with contrabassoon and double bass), Timothy Foley (conductor)
fields.note: The booklet marks the players participating in the Rossini: flute, two oboes, two B-flat clarinets, two bassoons, contrabassoon, two horns and string bass. No trumpet or cello performance is attributed to this transcription.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Wind-ensemble transcription attributed to Wenzel Sedlak, adapted for the Marine Band’s Grand Scenes recording
fields.note: The booklet explicitly says the attribution to Sedlak has not been conclusively proved. The overture comes from a fifteen-movement suite preserved at the Augustinian monastery in Brno. For this recording, the flute part was modified using Rossini’s orchestral part, two added trumpet parts were removed, and contrabassoon and string bass reinforced the bass. This is a small wind ensemble with double bass, not Rossini’s original full orchestral scoring.

composer.background:
On 20 February 1816, at Rome’s Teatro Argentina, a barber came on stage announcing that everyone needed him. Figaro could shave a chin, deliver a letter and arrange a marriage, and he called out his own name so many times that the part tested even his singer. The opera was advertised as Almaviva, ossia L’inutile precauzione. Its first night failed. Within a few performances the public had changed its mind about Rossini’s Barber of Seville.

Gioachino Rossini was born in Pesaro on 29 February 1792. His father Giuseppe played horn and trumpet; his mother Anna Guidarini became a professional singer. The boy travelled with them as they worked. In Lugo, from 1802, the priest Giuseppe Malerbi taught him composition and introduced him to Haydn and Mozart. At Bologna’s Liceo Musicale, which he entered in 1806, Rossini studied cello, piano and counterpoint. Before he composed operas he worked in the theatre as a musician, singer and keyboard player.
